title: Least Number of Unique Integers After K Removals
description: Minimize distinct values remaining after removing exactly k elements, using a greedy sort-by-frequency elimination strategy.

sections.title: Least Number of Unique Integers After K Removals

content.title: Least Number of Unique Integers After K Removals

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an integer array arr and an integer k, remove exactly k elements from the array (choosing which ones freely) to minimize the number of distinct values remaining. Return that minimum count.

blocks.caption: Fully removing the rarest value groups first eliminates the most distinct values for the fewest total removals.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","arr[] (can have repeated values), k (exact number of elements to remove)"],["Goal","Minimize the number of distinct values remaining after removing exactly k elements"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

To eliminate a distinct value entirely, EVERY occurrence of it must be removed. To minimize the remaining distinct count for a fixed removal budget, always target the value with the FEWEST occurrences first, since it costs the least to eliminate completely. This is a classic greedy-by-frequency problem.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Sorting by frequency (not by value) and greedily consuming the smallest groups first is the same idea as Task Scheduler's frequency-driven greedy reasoning, just applied to elimination instead of scheduling.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture jars of marbles, one color per jar, holding however many marbles of that color exist in the array. To empty out (eliminate) a color entirely, every marble in that jar must be removed. With a limited removal budget, emptying the jar with the FEWEST marbles first eliminates a color for the cheapest possible cost, always the best use of the budget.

blocks.caption: Emptying the smallest jars first eliminates the most colors for a given budget.

items: Count the frequency of every distinct value.
Greedily "spend" the removal budget k on the smallest frequency groups first, fully eliminating each one (reducing the distinct count by one) as long as the budget covers its full frequency.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
arr = [4,3,1,1,3,3,2], k = 3. Frequencies: 4 appears 1 time, 1 appears 2 times, 3 appears 3 times, 2 appears 1 time. Sorted frequencies: [1, 1, 2, 3].

blocks.content: {"headers":["Frequency group processed","k remaining before","Fits within budget?","k remaining after","Unique count"],"rows":[["1 (either 4 or 2)","3","yes (1 <= 3)","2","3 (started at 4)"],["1 (the other of 4 or 2)","2","yes (1 <= 2)","1","2"],["2 (value 1)","1","no (2 > 1), stop","1","2 (final)"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: After removing both single-occurrence values (4 and 2) using 2 of the 3 removal budget, the last removal is not enough to eliminate the frequency-2 group (value 1), so 2 distinct values remain: 1 and 3, matching the expected output of 2.
5. How Should We Think?

A direct simulation repeatedly finds the current smallest-frequency value and removes one occurrence of it, one at a time, for k total removal steps. This directly implements the greedy rule but rescans the frequency map at every single step.

Sorting the frequencies once up front lets the greedy elimination proceed in a single pass: process frequency groups in ascending order, fully consuming the budget on the smallest group before moving to the next, stopping the moment the budget can no longer fully eliminate the current group.
6. Brute Force Solution
Repeatedly find the value with the current smallest frequency and remove one occurrence, k times total.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(k * d)","d is the number of distinct values, rescanned every one of the k removal steps"],["Space","O(d)","The frequency map"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Rescanning for the current minimum on every single removal step is unnecessary once frequencies are sorted once up front.
8. Optimize the Solution

Count frequencies once, then sort them ascending. Walk the sorted frequencies; for each, if the remaining budget k is at least that frequency, spend k on fully eliminating it (decrementing k and the unique count); otherwise, the budget cannot fully eliminate this or any later (larger) group, so stop.

items: Sort the frequency values, O(d log d).
Walk sorted frequencies once, greedily eliminating groups the budget can fully afford, O(d).

blocks.text: 9. Optimized Solution
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, repeated min-scan","O(k * d)","O(d)"],["Optimized, sort frequencies then single pass","O(n + d log d)","O(d)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Minimizing distinct values under a removal budget is a greedy-by-frequency problem: always target the smallest frequency group first.
Sorting frequencies once, rather than repeatedly rescanning for the current minimum, turns a per-step search into a single linear sweep.
The moment the budget cannot fully afford the current (smallest remaining) group, no later group can be afforded either, since frequencies are sorted ascending.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Least Number of Unique Integers After K Removals is solved by counting frequencies, sorting them ascending, and greedily eliminating the smallest frequency groups first while the removal budget allows, since fully eliminating the rarest values first always minimizes the remaining distinct count.
